title: Romans Chapter 13 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Romans chapter 13 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Romans Chapter 13 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Romans Chapter 13.

questions.question: In Romans 13, which of the following appears FIRST in the chapter?
options: Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers.
For he is the minister of God to thee for good.
Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God.
Wherefore ye must needs be subject, not only for wrath.
questions.correctAnswer: Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers.
questions.explanation: This statement is the very first verse in the chapter, Romans 13:1.

questions.question: According to Romans 13:2, what happens to those who resist the power?
options: They shall receive to themselves damnation.
They will be protected by God.
questions.correctAnswer: They shall receive to themselves damnation.
questions.explanation: This is stated directly in Romans 13:2, indicating the consequence of resisting the power.

questions.question: Who are rulers not a terror to, according to Romans 13:3?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:3 clearly states that rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil.

questions.question: What should one do to have praise from the power as stated in Romans 13:3?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:3 encourages doing good to receive praise from the power.

questions.question: According to Romans 13:4, what is the ruler a minister of God for?
options: To execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
questions.correctAnswer: To execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
questions.explanation: Romans 13:4 states that the ruler is a minister of God to execute wrath on evildoers.

questions.question: What must one be subject to, according to Romans 13:5?
options: Both for wrath and for conscience sake.
questions.correctAnswer: Both for wrath and for conscience sake.
questions.explanation: Romans 13:5 indicates that one must be subject for both reasons.

questions.question: What does Romans 13:1 say about powers?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:1 states that the powers that be are ordained of God.

questions.question: According to Romans 13:4, what should one be afraid of if they do evil?
questions.explanation: This is mentioned in Romans 13:4, indicating that the ruler bears not the sword in vain.

questions.question: What is the consequence of resisting the ordinance of God as per Romans 13:2?
options: They shall receive to themselves damnation.
questions.correctAnswer: They shall receive to themselves damnation.
questions.explanation: This is explicitly stated in Romans 13:2, outlining the serious consequence of resisting authority.

questions.question: What should one not be afraid of according to Romans 13:3?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:3 suggests that rulers are not a terror to good works, implying one should not fear doing good.

questions.question: According to Romans 13:5, why is it necessary to be subject to the higher powers?
options: Not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake.
questions.correctAnswer: Not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake.
questions.explanation: This is stated in Romans 13:5, highlighting the dual reasons for being subject to authority.

questions.question: True or False: According to Romans 13:1, there is no power but of God.
questions.explanation: Romans 13:1 states that there is no power but of God, affirming this truth.

questions.question: True or False: Romans 13:4 states that the ruler is a minister of God for good.
questions.explanation: This is mentioned in Romans 13:4, indicating the role of the ruler as a minister of God for good.

questions.question: True or False: According to Romans 13:3, rulers are a terror to good works.
questions.explanation: Romans 13:3 states that rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil, making this statement false.

questions.question: True or False: Romans 13:2 indicates that resisting power leads to reward.
questions.explanation: Romans 13:2 states that resisting power leads to damnation, not reward, making this statement false.

medium.title: Romans Chapter 13 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Romans Chapter 13 to real-life situations.

questions.question: What should we pay tribute for, according to Romans 13:6?
questions.explanation: This answer is correct as Romans 13:6 states that we should pay tribute because those in authority are God's ministers, attending continually to their duties.

questions.question: What does Romans 13:7 promise will happen if someone pays tribute as commanded in Romans 13:6?
questions.explanation: By paying tribute, individuals are honoring those in authority, which aligns with the promise of receiving honor in return, as inferred from Romans 13:7.

questions.question: What does Romans 13:8 instruct us not to do?
questions.explanation: According to Romans 13:8, we are instructed not to owe anything to anyone, which emphasizes the importance of love over debt.

questions.question: What does Romans 13:9 summarize as a key principle of the law?
options: Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself
Thou shalt not bear false witness
questions.correctAnswer: Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself
questions.explanation: Romans 13:9 indicates that the essence of the law is encapsulated in loving one’s neighbor, fulfilling the commandments.

questions.question: According to Romans 13:10, what does love not do?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:10 states that love does no harm to a neighbor, highlighting love as the fulfillment of the law.

questions.question: How should we respond to higher powers according to Romans 13:1?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:1 teaches that every soul should be subject to higher powers, as they are ordained by God.

questions.question: What is the consequence mentioned in Romans 13:2 for resisting the power?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:2 states that resisting power results in receiving damnation, emphasizing the importance of obedience to authority.

questions.question: What type of behavior do rulers not terrorize, according to Romans 13:3?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:3 clarifies that rulers are not a terror to good works, reinforcing the idea that good behavior is commendable.

questions.question: What should one be afraid of if they do evil, according to Romans 13:4?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:4 explains that one should be afraid of the authority if they do evil, as they are appointed to execute wrath.

questions.question: Why should we be subject to authorities according to Romans 13:5?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:5 highlights that we must be subject not only for wrath but also for the sake of our conscience, underscoring moral responsibility.

questions.question: What is the overarching principle behind fulfilling the law, as stated in Romans 13:10?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:10 indicates that love is the essence that fulfills the law, showing that love is paramount in Christian ethics.

questions.question: According to Romans 13:8, what is the only debt we should have?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:8 teaches that we should owe no one anything except love, which is a continuous obligation.

questions.question: True or False: Romans 13:6 states that rulers are God's ministers attending to their own interests.
questions.explanation: This statement is false because Romans 13:6 clarifies that rulers are God's ministers attending continually upon God's commands, not their own interests.

questions.question: True or False: Romans 13:9 lists several commandments that relate to loving one's neighbor.
questions.explanation: This statement is true as Romans 13:9 outlines commandments that emphasize the importance of love towards one’s neighbor.

questions.question: True or False: Romans 13:3 suggests that rulers are a terror to good works.
questions.explanation: This statement is false because Romans 13:3 specifically states that rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil.

hard.title: Romans Chapter 13 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Romans Chapter 13.

questions.question: According to Romans 13:11, what should believers do because 'now is our salvation nearer than when we believed'?
options: Flee from the wrath to come
Build up the body of Christ
questions.explanation: Romans 13:11 states that it is high time to awake out of sleep because our salvation is nearer than when we believed.

questions.question: In Romans 13:12, what metaphor is used to describe the transition from sin to righteousness?
options: Casting off the works of darkness and putting on the armour of light
Crossing the Red Sea on dry ground
Shedding old skin like a snake
Climbing a mountain to see the Promised Land
questions.correctAnswer: Casting off the works of darkness and putting on the armour of light
questions.explanation: Romans 13:12 uses the metaphor of night being far spent and day at hand, urging believers to cast off works of darkness and put on the armour of light.

questions.question: Romans 13:13 commands believers to walk honestly 'as in the day.' Which of the following behaviors is NOT listed as something to avoid?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:13 lists rioting, drunkenness, chambering, wantonness, strife, and envying as behaviors to avoid but does not mention fasting and prayer.

questions.question: What does Paul instruct believers to 'put on' in Romans 13:14 to avoid fulfilling the lusts of the flesh?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:14 instructs believers to put on the Lord Jesus Christ and not make provision for the flesh to fulfill its lusts.

questions.question: According to Romans 13:11, what is the relationship between 'knowing the time' and spiritual alertness?
options: Knowing the time compels one to awake out of sleep
Knowing the time allows one to rest comfortably
Knowing the time means avoiding all worldly affairs
Knowing the time justifies delay in repentance
questions.correctAnswer: Knowing the time compels one to awake out of sleep
questions.explanation: Romans 13:11 connects awareness of the time with the necessity to awake out of sleep, indicating urgency for spiritual alertness.

questions.question: In Romans 13:12, the phrase 'the night is far spent, the day is at hand' employs which literary device?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:12 uses metaphor comparing spiritual darkness to night and righteousness to day, signifying the nearness of salvation.

questions.question: What does the Greek word 'panoplia' in Romans 13:12 mean?
questions.explanation: The Greek word 'panoplia' (Romans 13:12) means 'full armour,' referring to the complete protective gear metaphorically used for spiritual readiness.

questions.question: Which literary technique is prominently used in Romans 13:11-14 to emphasize the contrast between darkness and light?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:11-14 employs antithesis by juxtaposing darkness and light, sleep and awakening, flesh and Christ to highlight moral contrasts.

questions.question: Which Old Testament passage echoes the theme of loving one's neighbor as found in Romans 13:9?
questions.explanation: Leviticus 19:18 commands to love your neighbor as yourself, which is echoed in Romans 13:9 as fulfilling the law.

questions.question: Romans 13:1 speaks about submission to higher powers. Which New Testament passage also discusses submission to authorities?
questions.explanation: 1 Peter 2:13-17 similarly instructs believers to submit to authorities as instituted by God, paralleling Romans 13:1.

questions.question: What verse immediately precedes Romans 13:11 and discusses the fulfillment of the law through love?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:10 immediately precedes 13:11 and states that love works no ill to a neighbor and fulfills the law.

questions.question: How does Romans 13:14's command to 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' typologically relate to Old Testament priestly garments?
options: It symbolizes righteous identity and sanctification as priestly garments did for priests
It represents physical armor used in battles
It refers to wearing animal skins for protection
It is a metaphor for legalistic adherence to the law
questions.correctAnswer: It symbolizes righteous identity and sanctification as priestly garments did for priests
questions.explanation: Romans 13:14's figurative language of 'putting on' Christ parallels Old Testament typology where priestly garments symbolized sanctification and righteous identity.

questions.question: Which Greek word for 'lusts' in Romans 13:14 reflects strong desire or passion, often of a sinful nature?
questions.explanation: The Greek word 'epithumia' in Romans 13:14 means strong desire or lust, often indicating sinful cravings of the flesh.

questions.question: Romans 13:8 commands, 'Owe no man anything, but to love one another.' This is an example of which literary device?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:8 uses inclusio by framing the concept of debt both literally and spiritually, emphasizing love as the ultimate debt.

questions.question: True or False: Romans 13:14 instructs believers to make provision for the flesh to fulfill its lusts.
questions.explanation: Romans 13:14 explicitly commands not to make provision for the flesh to fulfill its lusts.

theological.title: Romans Chapter 13 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Romans Chapter 13 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What doctrine does Romans 13:1 teach about God's sovereignty?
options: All earthly powers are ordained by God
Human governments are independent from God
God permits evil rulers without purpose
Power is derived from human consensus
questions.correctAnswer: All earthly powers are ordained by God
questions.explanation: Romans 13:1 states that 'there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God,' affirming God's sovereign ordination of all governing authorities.

questions.question: What doctrine about human responsibility under government does Romans 13:2 teach?
options: Resisting governing authorities is resisting God's ordinance
Governments should always be disobeyed for personal freedom
Civil disobedience is justified in all cases
Government authority is irrelevant to Christian conduct
questions.correctAnswer: Resisting governing authorities is resisting God's ordinance
questions.explanation: Romans 13:2 warns that 'whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God,' highlighting the theological principle of submission to divinely ordained authorities.

questions.question: What doctrine about the role of government is taught in Romans 13:4?
options: Government ministers as God's agents to execute wrath on evildoers
Government has no role in punishing evil
Government is primarily for promoting wealth
Government should avoid all use of force
questions.correctAnswer: Government ministers as God's agents to execute wrath on evildoers
questions.explanation: Romans 13:4 describes rulers as 'the minister of God... a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil,' teaching that government serves a divine punitive role.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Romans 13:1 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:1 reveals God's sovereignty by showing that all powers are ordained by Him, underscoring His supreme authority over earthly rulers.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is highlighted in Romans 13:4 by describing government as God's minister to punish evil?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:4 emphasizes God's justice, manifested through governing authorities acting to punish wrongdoing as His ministers.

questions.question: How does Romans 13:8–10 connect to the broader biblical theme of the law of love found in the Old and New Testaments?
options: It summarizes all commandments as fulfilled in love for neighbor
It nullifies the Old Testament law entirely
It emphasizes ritual observance over love
questions.correctAnswer: It summarizes all commandments as fulfilled in love for neighbor
questions.explanation: Romans 13:9–10 shows that love is the fulfilling of the law, echoing Leviticus 19:18 and Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 22:37-40 about loving neighbor as oneself.

questions.question: In what way does Romans 13:11–14 prepare believers for ethical living in anticipation of Christ's return as portrayed in the eschatological narrative?
options: By urging urgent sanctification and putting on Christ as armor of light
By encouraging indulgence in fleshly desires
By focusing only on government obedience
By postponing holiness until after salvation
questions.correctAnswer: By urging urgent sanctification and putting on Christ as armor of light
questions.explanation: Romans 13:11–14 calls believers to awaken from spiritual sleep and to clothe themselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, preparing them ethically for the imminent salvation, consistent with eschatological exhortations elsewhere (cf. 1 Thessalonians 5:6).

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Romans 13:1 and Romans 13:4 teach about God's use of human authorities?
options: God ordains human authorities to maintain justice and punish evil
Human authorities act independently of God
God only uses angels to execute judgment
Government is a human invention without divine purpose
questions.correctAnswer: God ordains human authorities to maintain justice and punish evil
questions.explanation: Romans 13:1 states powers are ordained by God, and Romans 13:4 explains rulers are ministers of God to execute wrath on evildoers, teaching that God uses human authorities to uphold justice.

questions.question: What combined doctrine about love and law is taught in Romans 13:8 and Romans 13:10?
options: Love fulfills the law by working no harm to neighbors
Law is superior to love in ethical priority
Love is a feeling unrelated to moral commands
questions.correctAnswer: Love fulfills the law by working no harm to neighbors
questions.explanation: Romans 13:8 commands love as the fulfillment of the law, and 13:10 explains love 'worketh no ill to his neighbour,' summarizing the moral law in the principle of love.

questions.question: What combined doctrine about conscience and submission is taught by Romans 13:5 and Romans 13:7?
options: Submission to authorities is both for conscience sake and to render all dues
Tribute and honor are optional for Christians
Submission is only for fear of punishment, not conscience
questions.correctAnswer: Submission to authorities is both for conscience sake and to render all dues
questions.explanation: Romans 13:5 instructs submission 'for wrath, but also for conscience sake,' while 13:7 commands rendering tribute, custom, fear, and honor to whom they are due, teaching comprehensive submission motivated by conscience and duty.

questions.question: Sceptics claim Romans 13:1-7 endorses uncritical obedience to all governments, including tyrannical ones. What does Romans 13:1-7 actually teach?
options: Governments are ordained by God for good, and obedience is required, but their authority is limited to punishing evil
Christians must obey all government commands without question
Government power is absolute and unlimited
God endorses all actions of government regardless of morality
questions.correctAnswer: Governments are ordained by God for good, and obedience is required, but their authority is limited to punishing evil
questions.explanation: Romans 13:1-4 teaches that rulers are God’s ministers for good and to punish evil, implying their authority is for just governance, not tyrannical evil, thus obedience is bounded by justice.

questions.question: What doctrine about the believer's ethical vigilance is taught in Romans 13:11?
options: Believers must awaken from spiritual sleep because salvation is nearer
Believers should delay ethical living until salvation is complete
questions.correctAnswer: Believers must awaken from spiritual sleep because salvation is nearer
questions.explanation: Romans 13:11 exhorts believers to 'awake out of sleep' recognizing that salvation is nearer than before, emphasizing ongoing ethical vigilance.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Romans 13:6 demonstrate by instructing payment of tribute to rulers as God’s ministers?
questions.explanation: Romans 13:6 explains rulers are God’s ministers attending continually to governing, showing God’s providential care over human institutions.

questions.question: What combined doctrine about sanctification and Christlikeness is taught in Romans 13:12 and Romans 13:14?
options: Believers must cast off works of darkness and put on the Lord Jesus Christ to overcome fleshly lusts
Sanctification is unrelated to Christ's person
Fleshly desires should be indulged as part of grace
questions.correctAnswer: Believers must cast off works of darkness and put on the Lord Jesus Christ to overcome fleshly lusts
questions.explanation: Romans 13:12 urges casting off darkness and putting on armor of light, and 13:14 commands putting on the Lord Jesus Christ and not fulfilling fleshly lusts, combining sanctification and Christlikeness.

questions.question: How does Romans 13:3 contribute to the biblical doctrine of the role of government in promoting good and restraining evil?
options: Rulers are terror to evildoers but not to those who do good
Governments are neutral and indifferent to morality
Governments promote evil by their nature
Rulers should only reward the righteous, not punish evil
questions.correctAnswer: Rulers are terror to evildoers but not to those who do good
questions.explanation: Romans 13:3 explains rulers are 'not a terror to good works, but to the evil,' affirming government’s role in restraining evil and encouraging good.
